title: ‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring voters back in Labour heartlands?

paragraphs.en: Labour marked its worst performance in more than 50 years when voters went to the polls in Barnsley in May, but 100 days on from those seismic local elections, the political landscape has shifted drastically.
Could the South Yorkshire town, where Reform UK reaped the benefits of dissatisfaction with Labour, prove to be a test case for whether the governing party has turned the tide?
Labour had run Barnsley’s council since its inception in 1974, but was left with just 11 councillors after Reform triumphed with 42 seats.

“I knew that it would be the most challenging set of elections that we’ve ever faced in Barnsley’s history,” said the councillor James Higginbottom, the new Labour group opposition leader. “What I didn’t necessarily expect was the scale of the Reform victory.”

Catastrophic results in places such as Barnsley were a catalyst for Keir Starmer’s resignation. He has been replaced as prime minister by the former mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham, who won the Labour leadership uncontested after a landslide byelection victory.

Meanwhile, the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, is facing scrutiny over his financial affairs. While he was decisively re-elected in Clacton on Thursday, after he called a byelection in protest over a parliamentary standards investigation into his financial gifts, the contest was largely viewed as a sideshow after other major parties declined to stand. The parliamentary standards investigation has now resumed .
Labour is now ahead in the polls for the first time since March 2025, with a YouGov poll on Monday giving Labour a two-point lead, at 24 points to Reform’s 22.

Many in Barnsley used their vote in May to punish Starmer’s government, and while almost everyone the Guardian spoke to there this week said it was too early to judge the Reform council on their record, the new national political picture appears to be enticing at least some back to Labour.
